metadata.title: Parental Involvement in Selected PISA Countries and Economies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses PISA 2009 microdata with a parental questionnaire administered in 14 countries/economies, but it does not report the specific complex-sampling weight variables or replicate-weight procedures used in the analyses. The study focuses on associations between parental involvement indicators and student outcomes (reading performance, enjoyment of reading, and awareness of effective summarising strategies), which in PISA are typically estimated with the complex survey design and (for cognitive outcomes) plausible-value methodology. Because the working paper does not document whether sampling weights were applied, the safest interpretation is that the authors used standard PISA analytical practices but did not provide the weight variable names or replicate design details in the excerpt provided. Analysts using the OECD/PISA database should apply the official PISA student weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors for cross-national comparisons, and should ensure PV-based estimation for reading performance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The working paper reports relationships between parental involvement and PISA outcomes, but the provided text does not specify how missing questionnaire responses were handled (e.g., complete-case vs imputation) or how missingness was treated in the regression models. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets commonly contain item nonresponse in both student and parental questionnaires, and the choice of missing-data strategy can affect cross-national estimates and subgroup comparisons. The excerpt also does not document the exact PV estimation procedure for reading performance, so the PV and missing-data handling cannot be fully audited from the text provided.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2009 student data linked to the optional parental questionnaire, restricting the analytic sample to the 14 countries/economies that administered the parental questionnaire in 2009. Poland is explicitly excluded from parental-involvement results because it did not administer the parental-involvement section, so Poland’s involvement outcomes are not included. The paper further focuses on reading-related outcomes at age 15 (reading performance, enjoyment of reading, and awareness of effective summarising strategies) and on parental involvement indicators measured for early primary (ISCED 1) and for the adolescent period (home-based and school-based involvement). The excerpt does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing parental questionnaire items, missing ESCS, or response-quality filters).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes cross-national patterns of parental involvement using PISA 2009, where 14 countries/economies administered an optional parental questionnaire. The study links parental involvement indicators to three student outcomes at age 15: reading performance (cognitive), enjoyment of reading (non-cognitive motivation), and awareness of effective summarising strategies (a metacognitive/learning-strategy indicator). It reports that some forms of involvement—especially reading to children when they are young, discussing complex social/political issues, and parents reading for enjoyment—show stronger positive associations with both cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes than more school-based or homework-help oriented involvement. The paper also documents substantial cross-country variation and within-country inequalities in parental involvement by socioeconomic status and immigrant background, and it frames how parental involvement may mediate performance gaps through composition and differential strength. Causality is not claimed because PISA is observational and the excerpt does not document PV estimation and missing-data handling details.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper that reports descriptive and regression-based associations rather than training or evaluating machine-learning predictive models. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques is empty) and there are no ML target-variable performance metrics to populate in main_findings. The excerpt also does not provide the technical details needed to extract PV handling and missing-data procedures precisely, so those fields are necessarily limited.
